title: Memory: Stack & Heap
tagline: Where your variables actually live — and why confusing value with reference silently breaks code.

sections.content:
Every variable you declare and every object you create reserves space somewhere in RAM. That *somewhere* is not random — the runtime splits memory into two regions with entirely different rules: the **stack** and the **heap**. Understanding the split explains why copying an object can surprise you, why functions clean up after themselves automatically, and why `const` does not mean immutable.

This topic underpins call-stack errors, garbage collection, value-vs-reference semantics, and the performance of data structures. It is a reliable interview question and a foundation for every topic that follows.

sections.caption: The runtime splits memory into a small, fast stack (function frames) and a large heap (objects). Primitives live on the stack; objects live on the heap, accessed via references.

sections.title: A Restaurant Kitchen
sections.content:
Picture a restaurant kitchen. Each chef (function) gets a small, numbered prep station — that is the **stack frame**. The station holds exactly what the chef needs right now: the recipe card (return address), a few pre-measured bowls (parameters and local primitives). When the chef finishes, the station is cleared instantly and handed to the next cook.

The walk-in refrigerator is the **heap**. Large items that do not fit on the station (a whole leg of lamb, a giant vat of stock) are stored there. The chef keeps a *ticket* with the fridge location — that ticket is a **reference**. Multiple chefs can hold tickets to the same item, meaning they all see the same data. Someone must track when no chef needs an item and throw it out — that is **garbage collection**.

The **stack** is a contiguous, LIFO region managed by the CPU and runtime. Every function call pushes a **stack frame** containing parameters, local primitive variables, and a return address. When the function returns the frame is popped — the stack pointer simply moves back. No per-variable cleanup loop runs; that is why stack allocation is essentially free. The catch: the stack is small (typically 1–8 MB per thread). Deeply nested calls can exhaust it, producing a **stack overflow**.

The **heap** is a large, unstructured memory pool. Allocating on the heap means requesting a block, finding a free chunk, and returning a pointer to it. In managed languages like JavaScript a **garbage collector** periodically marks heap objects that are no longer reachable from any live reference and reclaims them. Heap access is slower than stack access because it involves pointer indirection and can cause CPU cache misses.

In JavaScript, **primitives** — `number`, `string`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, `symbol`, `bigint` — are stored *by value*. Assigning or passing a primitive copies the actual value; the copy is independent. **Objects, arrays, and functions** are heap-allocated. A variable holds a *reference* (memory address), not the object itself. Assigning an object to a new variable copies the reference, so both variables alias the same heap data — a mutation through one is visible through the other. This is why `const obj = {}` does not make the object immutable: `const` prevents *reference reassignment*, not heap mutation.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Lines 4-7 show primitive (value) copy — two independent stack slots. Lines 10-13 show object (reference) copy — one heap object, two aliases. Spread (line 16) creates a new top-level object but does not recurse into nested references (line 20-23). `structuredClone()` (Node 17+, modern browsers) performs a true recursive deep copy for JSON-safe data.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Interview tip:** when asked 'stack vs heap?' lead with *lifetime*, not just speed. Stack memory has deterministic, automatic lifetime tied to the function call. Heap memory has indefinite lifetime managed by GC. Then add: JS primitives live on the stack (by value), objects on the heap (by reference). Finish with: `const` prevents reference reassignment but does not make heap data immutable — that trips up many mid-level candidates.

items: The **stack** is a small, fast, automatically managed LIFO region; each function call pushes a frame that is instantly reclaimed on return.
The **heap** is large and slower; objects persist there until no live reference remains and the garbage collector reclaims them.
JS **primitives** (number, string, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint) are copied by value — changes to the copy never affect the original.
JS **objects, arrays, and functions** are heap-allocated; variables hold references — two aliases to the same object see each other's mutations.
`const` blocks reference reassignment only; use `Object.freeze()` or `structuredClone()` to lock or truly copy heap data.

quiz.question: Where are a function's local primitive variables stored during execution?
options: On the heap, managed by the garbage collector
In the stack frame for that function call
In a global memory region shared by all functions
In CPU registers only, never in RAM
quiz.explanation: Each function call pushes a stack frame that holds its local primitives and parameters. The frame is popped and freed the instant the function returns — no GC needed.

quiz.question: What happens in memory when you write `let b = a` and `a` is a JavaScript number?
options: b holds a reference to the same memory location as a
b receives an independent copy of a's value
Both a and b are frozen
a is moved to the heap
quiz.explanation: Numbers are primitives. Assignment copies the value. b starts equal to a but is completely independent; changing b has no effect on a.

quiz.question: After `const x = { count: 0 }; const y = x; y.count = 5;`, what is `x.count`?
options: undefined
A TypeError is thrown
quiz.explanation: x and y hold the same reference to the same heap object. Mutating via y changes the value visible through x. Both read 5.

quiz.question: What does the garbage collector use to decide whether a heap object can be reclaimed?
options: How long the object has been alive
Whether the object is reachable from any live reference
The size of the object
Whether the object was declared with const or let
quiz.explanation: JavaScript's GC uses reachability (mark-and-sweep). An object is collected only when no live path from a root (global, stack variable, closure) leads to it.

quiz.question: Which JavaScript value type is stored by value rather than by reference?
options: An array
A function
A boolean
A plain object {}
quiz.explanation: Booleans are primitives — stored and passed by value. Arrays, functions, and plain objects are all heap-allocated and passed by reference.

quiz.question: What is the most likely cause of a 'Maximum call stack size exceeded' error?
options: Allocating a very large array on the heap
Infinite or very deep recursion filling the call stack
Mutating a const variable
Calling JSON.parse on an invalid string
quiz.explanation: Each function call pushes a stack frame. Unbounded recursion keeps pushing frames until the stack's size limit is exceeded — a stack overflow.

quiz.question: After `const obj = { a: 1 }; Object.freeze(obj); obj.a = 99;`, what is `obj.a`?
options: undefined
A ReferenceError is thrown
quiz.explanation: Object.freeze() makes own properties non-writable. The assignment is silently ignored in sloppy mode (throws TypeError in strict mode). obj.a stays 1.

quiz.question: You shallow-clone with `const clone = { ...original }`. A nested object inside original is then mutated. Is clone affected?
options: No — spread creates a full deep copy
Yes — nested objects are still shared references
Only if the nested object is an array
Only in strict mode
quiz.explanation: Spread copies top-level property values. If a value is itself a reference (nested object or array), the original and the clone share that same heap reference.

quiz.question: Why does `const arr = [1,2,3]; arr.push(4);` not throw a TypeError?
options: Arrays are special and ignore const
const only prevents reassigning the reference — mutating the heap array is fine
push() creates a new array, so arr is not really changed
const is only enforced in strict mode
quiz.explanation: const prevents `arr = somethingElse` (reassigning the reference). It does not prevent modifying the heap array that arr points to — push mutates the array in place.

quiz.question: Which method correctly performs a deep clone of a plain JSON-serializable object in modern JavaScript (Node 17+)?
options: Object.assign({}, original)
{ ...original }
structuredClone(original)
Object.freeze(original)
quiz.explanation: structuredClone() (Node 17+, modern browsers) recursively deep-copies an object. Object.assign and spread are shallow; Object.freeze makes an object immutable but does not clone it.
